title: Sparring: affinity heuristics & jitter notes (week of 2029-03-18)
content:
Attendees: Maya, Liam, Sofia, Diego, Priya

Quick summary (tl;dr):
- This week we ran a focused set of small-batch traffic experiments to test per-query shard affinity and its interaction with KV shadow cache hit rates.
- Observed an unexpected latency jitter when affinity assignments flip for hot keys — p50 unchanged, p95 up ~18% on short spikes, p99 up ~9%.
- Hypothesis: affinity churn causes transient cache ownership thrash + tiny GC/eviction storms at the kernel edge, which amplifies tail latency in low-latency paths.
- Action items: two short-term mitigations (soft-affinity decay & affinity quiesce window) and two longer-term follow-ups (slot-shepherd metrics + heap/evict tracing).

Context + motivation:
We want per-query shard affinity to reduce KV cache misses and improve throughput for sticky sessions. But the target is sub-10ms p50 for our smallest sequences — we can’t accept tail jitter for interactive flows. The sparring experiment attempts to push affinity aggressiveness while keeping batching intact, to see incremental wins and failure modes.

What we ran:
- Traffic: 10% of canary fleet (API route: /v1/generate-small) for non-priv customers, synthetic replay mixed with 20% real traffic.
- Duration: 72 hours (2029-03-15 06:00 -> 2029-03-18 06:00 UTC).
- Config delta compared to baseline: affinity_enabled=true, affinity_ttl=30s -> 10s for aggressive run, affinity_decay=linear, coalesce_window=3ms.
- Shadow cache telemetry enabled (KV-shadow-hit-rate, slot-ownership-change-rate).

Key observations (raw):
- KV shadow hit-rate improved from 67% -> 81% median during steady traffic bursts.
- p50 generation latency: 6.1ms (baseline 6.0ms) — acceptable.
- p95: 42ms -> 50ms spikes during reassign windows (~18% increase).
- p99: 126ms -> 137ms (9% increase).
- Correlation: spikes align with ownership-change-rate surges; ownership-change bursts preceded p95 spikes by ~40–120ms.
- Memory churn: host-level RSS had small but measurable blips (+2–4% over baseline) localized to kernels that gained ownership of hot slots.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Affinity churn leads to short-lived duplicate lookups and redundant prefill: when a slot moves, both old and new kernel attempt prefill -> double work -> temporary queueing.
2) Eviction ripple: aggressive affinity causes many micro-evictions at boundary slots which trigger writeback/cleanup tasks that briefly contend on allocator locks.
3) Scheduling jitter: the scheduler’s affinity resync path runs heavier maintenance tasks synchronously on ownership change which occasionally delays fast-path token generation.

Quick checks we did (and results):
- Added short traces around prefill path — observed overlapping prefill RPCs for ~12% of ownership changes.
- Enabled per-kernel lock contention counters — small spikes aligned with p95 events.
- Heap profiler sampling — not enough signal; need targeted heap traces during a spike.

Short-term mitigations (canary-ready):
1) Soft-affinity decay (rollout A): when affinity reassigns, new kernel enters a 250ms soft-handover where prefill is cooperative (prefill backoff + owner not allowed to aggressively evict). Expected to reduce duplicate work. Owner: Liam. ETA: 2029-03-23.
2) Affinity quiesce window (rollout B): suppress reassignment for a 500ms window after a slot gets prefetched + warmed (avoid flip-flops on noisy signals). Owner: Sofia. ETA: 2029-03-25.
Both mitigations are conservative configuration toggles; ready as feature flags in PR 4123.

Medium/long term follow-ups:
- Slot-shepherd observability: add metric for 'prefill-in-flight-per-slot' and 'ownership-change-latency' so we can see the handover tail. Owner: Diego. ETA: 2 sprints.
- Kernel-side async cleanup: convert some synchronous cleanup tasks into async background work with backpressure tokens to avoid blocking generation. Owner: Priya. ETA: planning in next sprint.
- Batch/coalesce tuning: experiment with coalesce_window increase during ownership-change windows (adaptive coalescing). Owner: Maya. ETA: spike next week.

Decisions made in session:
- Do NOT revert affinity globally; benefits to steady throughput justify targeted mitigations.
- Prioritize soft-affinity decay flag rollout to canary group first.
- For the next run, reduce coalesce_window to 1ms for a sub-cohort to confirm the scheduler-interaction hypothesis.

Open questions / risks:
- Will soft-affinity decay introduce stale cache corner-cases where two kernels think they own slot writes? Risk: low if cooperative prefill semantics are enforced.
- Is there an adversarial workload where quiesce windows cause livelock and underutilization? Need safety valves in autoscaler.
- Are we masking a deeper allocator contention bug rather than just affinity churn? If so, mitigation will be temporary.

Action items (concrete):
- Liam: prepare rollout PR for soft-affinity decay (feature flag + config docs) -> due 2029-03-22.
- Sofia: implement quiesce-window toggle + test harness for flapping keys -> due 2029-03-24.
- Diego: add slot-shepherd metrics to runtime telemetry (open ticket RW-8301) -> due 2029-04-05.
- Priya: prototype async cleanup worker and estimate perf delta -> spike 2029-03-26 to 2029-04-02.
- Maya: run a targeted sub-cohort with reduced coalesce_window 1ms and capture traces -> start 2029-03-24.

Notes to self / rough debugging tips for oncall:
- If you see p95 spikes correlated with ownership-change-rate, toggle affinity_decay to the conservative setting.
- Use 'slot-prefill-trace' span to identify overlapping prefill RPCs.
- On host-level RSS blips, check /proc/smaps and kernel allocator counters — small blips we saw were transient but worth capturing.

Closing thoughts (opinionated):
Affinity is attractive for steady-state cost wins, but our runtime needs to treat ownership changes as first-class events with lightweight handover semantics. The experiments show we can get the wins without full rollback, but it requires observability and a couple of small guardrails. The team feels confident: next week is about rolling soft-decay to canary and adding the shepherd metrics so we stop chasing ghosts in the telemetry.

End of notes.
